### Overview The Air Quality: Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) Station Measurements dataset is a global dataset that shows real-time air quality data from around the world for fine particulate matter (PM2.5). It presents data collected from government and international organizations at the station level. This means the data is more accurate to specific areas than national or regional data. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries and is being continually updated with new sources. PM2.5 are fine inhalable particles, with diameters that are generally 2.5 micrometers and smaller. These particles come in many sizes and shapes and can be made up of hundreds of different chemicals. Some are emitted directly from a source, such as construction sites or smokestacks, while others are created from complex reactions in the atmosphere. The size of these particles allows them to get deep into the lungs, and some may even get into the bloodstream. Numerous scientific studies have linked particle pollution exposure to a variety of health problems, including: premature death in people with heart or lung disease, nonfatal heart attacks, irregular heartbeat, aggravated asthma, decreased lung function, and increased respiratory symptoms. People with heart or lung diseases, children, and older adults are most likely to be affected by particle pollution exposure. OpenAQ is an open-source project to surface live, real-time air quality data from around the world. Its “mission is to enable previously impossible science, impact policy, and empower the public to fight air pollution.” Scientists, researchers, developers, and citizens can use these data to understand how air quality in different locations changes over time. Resource Watch also shows continually updated air quality data from OpenAQ on [inhalable particulates (PM10)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003bnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-10), [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cairqualityso2), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-O), [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003fnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-CO), and [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003gnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-BC_1). ### Methodology The fine particulate matter (PM2.5) station measurement dataset was produced and is continually updated by aggregating data from permanent outdoor air quality measures. Data was collected only from official sources, including government entities and international organizations. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries. For data to be included it had to meet three criteria: 1. The “raw” measurement data on physical particle concentration had to be available on the originating site. 2. The data needed to be at the “station level.” It is unacceptable if it is presented in an aggregated form for a city or region. 3. The data needed to be continuously updated at intervals between 10 minutes and 24 hours. After the data was collected it was put into tables. Data was collected using the source organization’s Air Quality Index (AQI) classifications. The final dataset was mapped in vector format at a subnational level with each measurement station showing local particle concentration. OpenAQ continually reviews each data source website for updated values and updates the dataset every hour. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows continually updated air quality data from OpenAQ on [inhalable particulates (PM10)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003bnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-10), [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cairqualityso2), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-O), [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003fnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-CO), and [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003gnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-BC_1). ### Overview This dataset shows global forecasts of probabilities for urban expansion through 2050. It separates the data into five shared socioeconomic pathways (SSPs), at a 5 kilometer (km) resolution. SSPs represent how different policy and societal choices will affect greenhouse gas emissions. The five scenarios used in this analysis are labeled as: - SSP1: Sustainability – Taking the Green Road (low challenges to mitigation and adaptation) - SSP2: Middle of the Road (medium challenges to mitigation and adaptation) - SSP3: Regional Rivalry – A Rocky Road (high challenges to mitigation and adaptation) - SSP4: Inequality – A Road Divided (low challenges to mitigation, high challenges to adaptation) - SSP5: Fossil-fueled Development – Taking the Highway (high challenges to mitigation, low challenges to adaptation) The dataset was created with information from a combination of five sources based on current urban land extent, population rates, Gross Domestic Product (GDP) information, and SSP scenarios. It is important to understand urban expansion because it can cause implications for warming, water scarcity, land use, and other environmental and social challenges. This dataset can be combined with other socioeconomic data to further examine the impacts of urban expansion. For instance, the dataset authors predicted urban expansion-induced warning in cities and suggested that it will increase extreme heat risks for about half of the future urban population. This will primarily affect communities in the tropical Global South that lack the adaptive capacity to meet environmental change. Policymakers can use this dataset to restrict or redistribute urban expansion and design strategies needed to mitigate Urban Heat Islands (UHIs) to reduce their negative impacts on human health, urban ecosystems, energy systems, and infrastructure. This dataset was published by Seto Lab, based at Yale School of the Environment. ### Methodology Researchers created this dataset using the URBANMOD-ZIPE model. The URBANMOD-ZIPE model was based on a 2012 global urban land change model, URBANMOD, and used to forecast pixels of urban expansion probabilities. The input data sources used for the updated model were: 1. urban land extent from the Global Human Settlement grid 2. urban population from the United Nations 3. Gross Domestic Product from the World Bank 4. future scenarios of the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) from the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis There were two phases to the model. Phase 1 predicted the quantities of urban land by 2050. This was done using a fixed effect panel regression model to relate urban land per capita to GDP per capita. Phase 2 utilized a land change model to allocate new urban lands to map pixels using slope, distance to roads, population density, and land covers as the drivers of land change. The final dataset was produced in raster format at a spatial resolution of 5 km. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1748-9326/ab4b71). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. Resource Watch has previously shown this data for urban expansion probabilities for 2030. This dataset was archived because the methodology has been changed and the global forecasts of probabilities for urban expansion through 2050 is now available. You can still access the archived data [here](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit005-Urban-Expansion-Probabilities_replacement). ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

### Overview This dataset tracks the number of people who have been internally displaced recently due to conflict, natural disasters, or development projects worldwide, and is updated daily. ”Internal displacement” refers to the forced movement of people within the country that they live in. Millions of people are forced to flee their homes each year due to conflict, violence, development projects, disasters, and climate change, and remain displaced within their countries of residence. Internally displaced persons (IDPs) can include both citizens and other habitual residents of the country, such as stateless persons. IDPs can include, but are not limited to - families caught between warring parties who had to flee their homes due to continuous attacks or threats; - residents of neighborhoods that have become unsafe or uninhabitable due to the impacts of weather-related, geophysical, or technological hazards; - indigenous communities forced from their ancestral lands to make way for the construction of dams and other infrastructure projects; - families pushed to leave their homes by constant harassment by local criminal gangs; - communities whose livelihoods have been severely impacted by drought and are unable to feed their families; and - communities from coastal, mountainous, or arid regions whose land and livelihoods were lost because of gradual environmental degradation linked to the impacts of climate change. Some of the typical needs and protection risks that arise in internal displacement include family separation, loss of documentation, loss of property, and further exposure to the risk of continued displacement. This dataset is produced by the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre (IDMC) with the aim of informing policy and operational decisions in order to reduce the risk of future displacement and improve the lives of IDPs worldwide. Resource Watch also shows IDMC estimates of the number of people displaced annually, aggregated to the national level. This data is available for displacements due to [natural disasters](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore?zoom=3&lat=-2.110674954311376&lng=7.456691250000007&basemap=dark&labels=light&layers=%255B%257B%2522dataset%2522%253A%2522ef9945f7-d934-4a88-a02a-570f14fffefc%2522%252C%2522opacity%2522%253A1%252C%2522layer%2522%253A%25223bda62f1-7146-4dd5-bf3f-d3bfae26d0d7%2522%257D%255D&page=1&sort=relevance&sortDirection=-1&search=soc.062a) and due to [conflict](https://preproduction.resourcewatch.org/data/explore?zoom=3&lat=-2.110674954311376&lng=7.456691250000007&basemap=dark&labels=light&layers=%255B%257B%2522dataset%2522%253A%25226974833b-004e-4b24-bdbc-ffbb779c1496%2522%252C%2522opacity%2522%253A1%252C%2522layer%2522%253A%2522cb5daeb3-80ef-4e6e-8ca8-5ed0d6170b3b%2522%257D%255D&page=1&sort=relevance&sortDirection=-1&search=soc.062b). ### Methodology Country analysts monitor displacements in near real-time on an event-by-event basis after IDMC learns of their occurrence. ### Overview This dataset shows forecasted sulfur dioxide (SO₂) concentrations at Earth's surface, modeled by the Whole Atmosphere Community Climate Model (WACCM). Sulfur dioxide is a colorless, reactive air pollutant with a strong odor. The gas is a respiratory irritant that can harm human health. According to the [Australian Department of Environment and Energy](https://www.environment.gov.au/protection/publications/factsheet-sulfur-dioxide-so2), sulfur dioxide irritates the nose, throat, and airways. It can cause shortness of breath, coughing, wheezing, or a tight feeling around the chest. High concentrations of sulfur dioxide can affect lung function, worsen asthma attacks, and worsen existing heart disease in sensitive groups. Most sulfur dioxide emissions come from the burning of coal, oil or gas for electricity and transportation; these fossil fuels contain sulfur, which is emitted as sulfur dioxide when burned. Sulfur dioxide does not contribute to global warming, but it [reacts easily](https://www.environment.gov.au/protection/publications/factsheet-sulfur-dioxide-so2) with other substances to form harmful compounds such as sulfuric acid and small sulfate particles. When sulfur dioxide reacts with water and oxygen, it [creates acid rain](https://www.epa.gov/acidrain/what-acid-rain). Acid rain has a number of [environmental impacts](https://www.ucsusa.org/clean-energy/coal-and-other-fossil-fuels/hidden-cost-of-fossils), including making lakes, rivers, wetlands and other water bodies more acidic, which can be harmful to fish and other aquatic wildlife. WACCM creates global forecasts for a variety of other air quality indicators, as well. While this dataset shows forecasted sulfur dioxide concentrations, Resource Watch also shows WACCM forecasts for [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-PM-25), [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-Black-Carbon), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-O), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-NO), and [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-CO). WACCM runs the model daily, and on their website you can find forecasted concentrations for each compound up to nine days into the future at three-hour time steps. WACCM was developed by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) and the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR). The data has global coverage at 1.9 x 2.5 degree resolution. ### Methodology WACCM is a comprehensive numerical model, driven by meteorological fields from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration’s (NASA) Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO) Goddard Earth Observing System Model, Version 5 (GEOS-5) model. The development of WACCM is an inter-divisional collaboration that unifies modeling from the High Altitude Observatory ([HAO](http://www2.hao.ucar.edu/)), the Atmospheric Chemistry Observations and Modeling ([ACOM](https://www2.acom.ucar.edu/)) Laboratory, and the Climate and Global Dynamics ([CGD](http://www2.cgd.ucar.edu/)) Laboratory. Upper atmospheric modeling from HAO, middle atmospheric modeling from ACOM, and tropospheric modeling from CGD are combined using the NCAR [Community Earth System Model (CESM)](http://www.cesm.ucar.edu/) as a common numerical framework. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://opensky.ucar.edu/islandora/object/articles%3A12836). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows WACCM forecasts for [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-PM-25), [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-Black-Carbon), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-O), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-NO), and [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-CO). It was created using multiple environmental variables as part of a study that attempts to utilize data from four Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPPC) emissions scenarios to determine the impact of climate change on coffee cultivation in coffee growing regions of Costa Rica. description: The World Database on Protected Areas (WDPA) is the most comprehensive global spatial data set on marine and terrestrial protected areas available. Protected area data are provided via Protected Planet, the online interface for the WDPA. The WDPA is a joint initiative of the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and the UN Environment Programme's World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC) to compile spatially referenced information about protected areas. The data are provided as shapefiles and updated monthly. Not all protected areas receive the same degree of protection. While some have strict guidelines designed to preserve intact ecosystems, others allow for sustainable land use, often including limited resource extraction. In addition, not all countries use the same terminology when designating a protected area. Universal management categories are designated by the IUCN that stipulate the level of protection for most protected areas. These categories are defined as follows: (Ia) Strict Nature Reserves: protected areas designed to preserve biodiversity and all geological features. Limited human use (e.g., scientific study, education) is allowed and carefully monitored. Strict nature reserves are often used to understand the impact of indirect human disturbance (e.g., burning fossil fuels) because of the area’s high level of preservation. (Ib) Wilderness Areas: protected areas managed to preserve ecosystem processes with limited human use. Wilderness areas cannot contain modern infrastructure (e.g., a visitor’s center), but they allow for local indigenous groups to maintain subsistence lifestyles. These areas are often established to restore disturbed environments. (II) National Parks: protected areas designed to preserve large-scale ecosystems and support human visitation. With conservation as a priority, these areas allow infrastructure and contribute to the local economy by providing opportunities for environmental educational and recreation. (III) National Monuments or Features: areas established to protect a specific natural feature (e.g., cave, grove) or human-made monument with significant historical, spiritual, or environmental importance and the immediate surroundings. Accordingly, natural monuments or features are typically smaller in area and have high human impact resulting from visitor traffic. (IV) Habitat and Species Management Areas: areas designed to conserve specific wildlife populations and/or habitats. Habitat and species management areas often exist within a larger ecosystem or protected area and are carefully managed (e.g., through hunting abatement or habitat restoration) to conserve a target species or habitat. (V) Protected Landscapes and Seascapes: protected areas with ecological, biological, or cultural importance that have been shaped by human use of the landscape. Protected landscapes and seascapes typically cover entire bodies of land or ocean and allow for a number of for-profit activities (e.g., ecotourism) in accordance with the region’s management plan. (VI) Protected Areas with Sustainable Use of Natural Resources: areas designed to manage natural resources and uphold the livelihoods of surrounding communities. These regions have a low level of human occupation, small-scale developments (i.e., not industrial), and part of the landscape in its natural condition. PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. ### Overview The Air Quality: Mexico City Carbon Monoxide (CO) Forecast dataset provides weather and air quality forecasts for Mexico City. This dataset represents the forecasted density of Carbon Monoxide in parts per billion (ppb). The forecast offers an hourly estimate on Carbon Monoxide density with a spatial resolution of 1 kilometer (km), encompassing Mexico CIty and its Metropolitan Area (MCMA). According to the [U.S. Center for Disease Control (CDC)](https://www.cdc.gov/co/faqs.htm), CO is released when fossil fuels are burned. Common household sources include grills, cars, fireplaces, and gas stoves that aren’t properly ventilated. Major sources of CO to outdoor air include cars, trucks and other fossil-fuel-burning machinery. Breathing air with a high concentration of carbon monoxide reduces oxygen availability in the bloodstream for critical organs like the heart and brain. Symptoms of CO poisoning include headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain, and confusion. As stated by [Mexico City Ministry of the Environment (SEDEMA)](http://www.aire.cdmx.gob.mx/descargas/publicaciones/flippingbook/informe_anual_calidad_aire_2017/mobile/informe_anual_calidad_aire_2017v3.pdf), the CO values in Mexico City have been decreasing over the last years, complying with the levels set by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the World Health Organization (WHO). The main source of CO in the MCMA is fossil-fuel-burning related to transport, making this pollutant a good indicator to monitor transport-related emissions in the region. Showcasing the spatial distribution of CO in the MCMA will provide insight about the way a city can produce information according to its needs while complementing global air quality models.The forecast helps the Mexico CIty government to issue health warnings based on the expected air quality for a given day, like recommending citizens to avoid open-air exercise or to limit their use of fossil fuel vehicles. The forecast was generated by SEDEMA with help from the Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC). SEDEMA provides a tool for the inhabitants of MCMA to make well-informed decisions about dangerous air pollution activity on a given day. SEDEMA works on five environmental issues: air quality and climate change, land conservation and biodiversity, sustainable urban infrastructure, water supply and quality, and environmental communication and education. ### Methodology The dataset is comprised of the following models: Weather: Estimates the weather conditions of the MCMA using data from global systems. It harnesses the [Weather Research and Forecasting Model-Advanced Research (WRF-ARW)](https://www.mmm.ucar.edu/weather-research-and-forecasting-model), which is a mesoscale numerical weather prediction system designed for both atmospheric research and operational forecasting applications. The model generates temperature, wind, rainfall and solar radiation, among other weather related indicators.. Emissions: This model makes use of emission inventories for the MCMA to estimate CO levels on an hourly basis, as well as its geospatial distribution. Chemical Transport: This model harnesses the outputs from the weather and emissions models as well as other chemical and physical mechanisms to simulate transformations in the atmosphere and the influence of weather dynamics in these processes. For this purpose, the [Community Multiscale Air Quality Modeling System (CMAQ)](https://www.cmascenter.org/cmaq/) is employed to forecast the behavior of the pollutants in the MCMA. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows forecasts for [Air Quality: Mexico City Sulfur Dioxide (SO₂) forecast ](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/59790e64-d95d-43fa-a124-5c7eb1cb4456), [Air Quality: Mexico City Ozone (O₃)Forecast](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/00d6bae1-e105-4165-8230-ee73a8128538), [Air Quality: Mexico City Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂) Forecast](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/918ba6bc-69ed-44fb-9b29-5fb445fdfef6), and [Air Quality: Mexico City Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5)Forecast](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7a34b770-83f9-4c6a-acb8-31edcff7241e) Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The Alert for Price Spices (ALPS) is generated by the World Food Programme (WFP). This alert indicates when prices of key staple food commodities have deviated from seasonal trends, and by how much. Early detection of food price increases can alert the international community to the possibility of current and future food insecurity in a region. Seasonal price trends are determined through reference to monthly commodity prices recorded in the WFP's Food and Commodity Price Database, which is collected by WFP country offices, national government agencies, and partner organizations. A linear regression is used to determine the contributions that 2 components make to seasonal price trends: the month of the year (related to harvest times) and the overall passage of time (related to population growth, inflation rates, etc.). The current ALPS value for a food commodity is the number of standard deviations the current price is above the commodity's expected price for that month. Based on this ALPS value, markets are assigned to 1 of 4 situations, where all nominal values are measured in standard deviations from the seasonal mean price: Normal, ALPS < 0.25 Stress, 0.25 < ALPS < 1 Alert, 1 < ALPS < 2 Crisis, ALPS >= 2 Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. ### Overview The Antarctic Sea Ice Extent dataset shows the extent of sea ice in the Antarctic for the latest month. Sea ice extent data was collected by satellite microwave sensing instruments at a spatial resolution of 25 kilometers (km). Data was collected daily and averaged at the end of each month to produce monthly ice extents. In this map, light blue represents locations where sea ice is currently present in the Antarctic region. This dataset can be used to understand the current Antarctic sea ice extent. Typically, Antarctic sea ice extent reaches its maximum in September and minimum in February. Although Antarctic sea ice extent varies significantly from year to year, the average ice extent has not changed over the past 40 years. According to the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)](https://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/understanding-climate-antarctic-sea-ice-extent), natural variability in the Southern Ocean and in atmospheric circulation patterns have a greater impact on Antarctic sea ice extent than climate change. However, climate change is disrupting wind patterns, currents and ocean temperatures across the globe. These changes may eventually impact Antarctic sea ice extent. The [National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC)](https://nsidc.org/) was founded in 1976 as the World Data Center for Glaciology. Over time, the NSIDC evolved to become a data distribution and research center specializing in remote sensing of cryospheric data such as snow, sea ice, frozen ground, ice sheets and glaciers. In addition to managing and distributing this data, the NSIDC creates and supports data access tools for its users. They also use the datasets for climate research and education. The NSIDC is part of University of Colorado Boulder’s [Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences (CIRES)](https://cires.colorado.edu/). It is supported by the [National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)](https://www.nasa.gov/), the [National Science Foundation (NSF)](https://www.nsf.gov/) and the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)](https://www.noaa.gov/). ### Methodology Data was collected daily at a spatial resolution of 25 km. The Special Sensor Microwave Imager/Sounder (SSMIS) instrument aboard the [Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP) satellites](https://www.ospo.noaa.gov/Operations/DMSP/index.html) measured the data. NSIDC used this satellite data to create the [Near-Real-Time DMSP SSMIS Daily Polar Gridded Sea Ice Concentrations (NRTSI)](https://nsidc.org/data/nsidc-0081) dataset. The Monthly Antarctic Sea Ice Extent dataset was generated from the NRTSI dataset. The SSMIS instrument senses microwave radiation emitted from the Earth's surface. The amount of microwave radiation emitted from an object depends on its physical properties, such as atomic composition and crystalline structure. The crystalline structure of ice typically emits more microwave energy than liquid ocean water, allowing SSMIS to easily distinguish sea ice from ocean water. SSMIS data was converted to [brightness temperature](https://glossary.ametsoc.org/wiki/Brightness_temperature), which is a descriptive measure of an object's radiation. Brightness temperature data was then converted to gridded ice concentration using the [NASA Team algorithm](https://nsidc.org/support/faq/nasa-team-vs-bootstrap-algorithm#NASATeam1). Gridded ice concentrations are the percentage of ice in a given cell. Each cell’s daily ice concentrations were averaged to produce monthly concentrations. If a cell contained more than 15% ice concentration, it was classified as ice. Otherwise, it was classified as water. Sea ice extent was delineated by the location where ice ends and the open ocean begins.
